paper.title_en: Scientific Background to the Nobel Prize in Physics 2026: For Decisive Contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the Discovery of High-Energy Neutrinos of Astrophysical Origin
paper.abstract_en:
This year, the Nobel Prize in Physics recognises the discovery of a diffuse flux of astrophysical
neutrinos, which extends to petaelectronvolt (PeV, $10^{15}$ eV) energies. Such neutrinos probe
cosmic-ray acceleration sites, where it is thought that highly relativistic protons or nuclei collide
with ambient matter or radiation to produce charged pions, which subsequently decay, producing
neutrinos. This milestone discovery in astroparticle physics has been made possible using data
recorded by the IceCube Neutrino Observatory – a cubic-kilometre–sized detector located at a
depth of ~2 km in the polar ice, close to the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station. IceCube is a
National Science Foundation (NSF)–managed research facility, operated as an international
collaboration involving ~450 people from 58 institutions in 14 countries.
Francis Halzen has long been the driving force behind the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. As
Principal Investigator from its beginnings, he has spearheaded the collective work by scientists
and engineers that resulted in a volume of instrumented Antarctic ice sufficiently large to detect
high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin. His scientific vision thus provides the basis for new
research in the future of this field.
